title: Restrictive and Interstitial Lung Diseases
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)

overview.intro: This chapter covers diseases that keep the lungs from expanding fully: surfactant failure in the newborn, diffuse alveolar damage in ARDS, scarring in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and related interstitial pneumonias, mineral dust and occupational exposures, sarcoidosis, drug-induced fibrosis, and restriction caused by the chest wall or muscles rather than the lung. Board questions give an exposure, a histologic pattern, a chest film, or a set of pulmonary function and blood gas values and ask you to name the disease and explain the finding. If you can say where the problem sits (alveolar lining, interstitium, or chest bellows) and how that changes compliance, DLCO, and the A-a gradient, you can reason through most of them.
prerequisites: Surfactant, surface tension, and the law of Laplace (PU-4)
Lung volumes, compliance, spirometry, and flow-volume loops
Alveolar gas equation, A-a gradient, and the five causes of hypoxemia (PU-7)
Granulomatous inflammation and wound repair by fibroblasts (general pathology)

connections.to: Fetal circulation and lung development (PU-1, CV-1)
connections.how: Surfactant matures late in gestation and the ductus arteriosus closes in response to oxygen, so prematurity links neonatal respiratory distress to a patent ductus.
Restrictive diseases are applied gas exchange: shunt in ARDS, diffusion limitation in fibrosis, and hypoventilation in chest wall and neuromuscular disease.
Chronic hypoxic vasoconstriction and loss of the capillary bed in fibrosis raise pulmonary artery pressure and lead to cor pulmonale.
Sarcoidosis and berylliosis are Th1 granulomatous diseases, and granuloma macrophages make calcitriol outside PTH control.
Asbestos causes pleural plaques, bronchogenic carcinoma, and mesothelioma as well as asbestosis.

terms.def: A disorder that reduces total lung capacity (TLC below about 80% of predicted) by stiffening the lung or limiting the chest wall or muscles, with a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio.
A phospholipid and protein mixture, chiefly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine, secreted by type II pneumocytes that lowers alveolar surface tension.
A pink, glassy layer of plasma proteins, fibrin, and necrotic epithelial debris lining alveolar ducts and alveoli after diffuse injury.
The histologic pattern of ARDS: injury to alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium with protein-rich edema and hyaline membranes.
The histologic pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: patchy subpleural and basal fibrosis of different ages with fibroblastic foci and honeycombing.
A small cluster of actively proliferating fibroblasts and myofibroblasts beneath injured epithelium, marking ongoing fibrosis.
End-stage remodeling in which fibrosis destroys alveoli and leaves clustered, thick-walled cystic spaces lined by bronchiolar epithelium.
Lung disease caused by inhaled inorganic dust, such as coal, silica, asbestos, or beryllium, and the lung's reaction to it.
An asbestos fiber coated with iron-containing protein, golden brown and beaded, that marks asbestos exposure.
A compact collection of epithelioid macrophages and multinucleated giant cells without central necrosis, typical of sarcoidosis and berylliosis.
Diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide, a measure of how readily gas crosses the alveolar-capillary membrane, reflecting surface area, membrane thickness, and capillary blood volume.
Alveolar PO2 calculated from the alveolar gas equation minus measured arterial PO2; about 5 to 15 mmHg in young adults on room air.

blocks.text: Surfactant is made by type II pneumocytes, which begin producing it late in the second trimester (often quoted as about 20 to 24 weeks of gestation); amounts usually become adequate at about 34 to 36 weeks. By the law of Laplace, the pressure tending to collapse an alveolus equals 2T/r, where T is surface tension and r is radius. Surfactant lowers T most in small alveoli, so alveoli of different sizes stay open together at end expiration. Without it, small alveoli collapse with every breath and the newborn must generate a large negative pressure to reopen them.

Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS, hyaline membrane disease) is surfactant deficiency. Prematurity is the main cause. Maternal diabetes delays maturation because fetal hyperinsulinemia, a response to maternal hyperglycemia, opposes the glucocorticoid stimulation of surfactant synthesis. Cesarean delivery without labor removes the labor-associated surge in fetal cortisol and catecholamines that speeds surfactant release and lung fluid clearance. Male sex also raises risk.

blocks.title: Surfactant deficiency to neonatal respiratory distress
steps: Immature type II pneumocytes make too little surfactant
High surface tension collapses alveoli at end expiration
Widespread atelectasis lowers compliance and work of breathing rises
Perfused but collapsed alveoli act as shunt; hypoxemia
Repeated collapse injures epithelium; plasma proteins leak
Fibrin and dead cells form hyaline membranes
blocks.caption: Atelectasis is the primary lesion; hyaline membranes are the consequence of the resulting epithelial and capillary injury.

blocks.text: Collapsed alveoli that remain perfused behave as an intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt, so hypoxemia responds poorly to added oxygen. Within minutes to hours of birth the infant shows tachypnea, expiratory grunting (closing the glottis to hold air in the lungs), nasal flaring, intercostal and subcostal retractions, and cyanosis. The chest film shows low lung volumes with a diffuse fine granular or ground-glass pattern and air bronchograms, because air-filled bronchi stand out against airless alveoli.
Predictable complications

The ductus arteriosus normally closes because arterial PO2 rises and prostaglandin E2 falls after birth. In NRDS, hypoxemia and acidosis keep the ductus open, and the premature ductus is also less responsive to oxygen, so a patent ductus arteriosus is common. As pulmonary resistance falls, blood shunts left to right through it and floods the stiff lungs.

The supplemental oxygen and positive-pressure ventilation needed to support these infants cause their own injury. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is chronic lung disease of the premature infant, with arrested alveolar and vascular development (fewer, larger alveoli) from oxygen free radicals, volume and pressure injury, and inflammation. Retinopathy of prematurity follows a two-step mechanism: high arterial PO2 suppresses vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and halts normal retinal vessel growth, then the avascular retina becomes hypoxic once oxygen is lowered, VEGF surges, and disorganized new vessels grow that can bleed, scar, and detach the retina.

blocks.predict: Why does raising inspired oxygen improve PaO2 only a little in a newborn with severe NRDS?
blocks.explain: The main cause of hypoxemia is shunt through perfused alveoli that are collapsed; blood passing them never contacts the added oxygen, and saturated blood from open alveoli cannot carry extra oxygen to compensate.
blocks.check: The paragraph on shunt and the flow figure.

blocks.text: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is noncardiogenic pulmonary edema caused by diffuse injury to the alveolar-capillary barrier. The barrier can be injured from the airway side (pneumonia, aspiration of gastric contents, inhalation injury, near drowning) or from the blood side (sepsis, which with pneumonia is among the most common causes, severe trauma with shock or multiple transfusions, and acute pancreatitis, in which circulating enzymes and cytokines injure capillaries).

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of ARDS
steps: Direct or systemic insult activates alveolar macrophages and endothelium
IL-1, TNF, and IL-8 recruit and activate neutrophils
Neutrophil proteases and oxygen radicals damage endothelium and type I pneumocytes
Protein-rich fluid floods the interstitium and alveoli
Edema fluid inactivates surfactant; alveoli collapse
Hyaline membranes line alveolar ducts
Shunt and stiff lungs cause refractory hypoxemia
blocks.caption: Neutrophils are the main effector cells; the leak is caused by barrier injury, not by high capillary pressure.

blocks.text: The histologic pattern is diffuse alveolar damage. In the first week (exudative phase) the alveolar walls are edematous and hyaline membranes line the alveolar ducts. Over the next one to three weeks (proliferative or organizing phase) type II pneumocytes proliferate to reline the alveoli and fibroblasts organize the exudate; some patients progress to interstitial fibrosis. Because the fluid is rich in protein from barrier failure, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is usually normal, which separates ARDS from cardiogenic edema, in which high left atrial pressure (wedge pressure above about 18 mmHg) pushes a protein-poor transudate across an intact barrier.

Flooded and collapsed alveoli remain perfused, so the dominant gas exchange defect is shunt, and hypoxemia responds poorly to oxygen. Compliance falls because fewer alveoli are open to receive each breath, and the chest film shows bilateral patchy or diffuse opacities. Inactivated surfactant adds atelectasis, and the stiff lungs force rapid, shallow breathing. Severity is graded by the ratio of arterial PO2 to the inspired oxygen fraction (PaO2/FiO2), normally above about 400 to 500.

blocks.title: Consensus (Berlin) criteria for ARDS
rows: Within 1 week of a known insult or new or worsening respiratory symptoms
Bilateral opacities not fully explained by effusion, collapse, or nodules
Not fully explained by heart failure or fluid overload
Oxygenation (with PEEP or CPAP of at least 5 cm H2O)
Mild: PaO2/FiO2 over 200 to 300; moderate: over 100 to 200; severe: 100 or less
blocks.caption: A PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 300 or less defines the oxygenation threshold; the older term acute lung injury has been retired.

blocks.title: Grading oxygenation in ARDS
blocks.text: A patient with septic shock has bilateral infiltrates and a normal echocardiogram. On FiO2 0.60 with PEEP of 10 cm H2O, PaO2 is 72 mmHg. PaO2/FiO2 = 72 / 0.60 = 120, which is moderate ARDS (over 100 to 200). Compare a healthy person on room air: 95 / 0.21 is about 450. The ratio corrects for the oxygen being given, which is why a PaO2 that looks acceptable can still mean severe gas exchange failure. Raising FiO2 to 1.0 raises PaO2 relatively little here because the defect is shunt.

sections.title: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and the usual interstitial pneumonia pattern

blocks.text: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a progressive fibrosing disease of unknown cause in older adults, usually over 60, more often men and smokers or former smokers. The current model is repeated microscopic injury to alveolar epithelium followed by abnormal repair in a susceptible lung. Susceptibility includes a common promoter variant of the mucin gene MUC5B and mutations that shorten telomeres (telomerase genes TERT and TERC), which impair renewal of type II pneumocytes.

blocks.title: Aberrant repair in IPF
steps: Repeated injury to alveolar epithelium (smoking, reflux, environmental)
Type II pneumocytes fail to restore the epithelium
Injured epithelium releases TGF-beta
Fibroblasts become myofibroblasts in fibroblastic foci
Excess collagen stiffens and distorts the interstitium
Alveoli are destroyed and honeycomb cysts form
blocks.caption: Fibrosis follows failed epithelial repair rather than a prominent inflammatory phase, so inflammation is mild in UIP.

blocks.text: Transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) is the central profibrotic signal: it drives fibroblast proliferation, conversion to contractile myofibroblasts, and collagen deposition while inhibiting matrix breakdown. The histologic pattern is usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP). Fibrosis is patchy and worst in the subpleural and basal lung. Its defining feature is temporal heterogeneity: dense old collagen, active fibroblastic foci, and normal lung lie side by side, because injury occurs at different times in different places. End-stage scarring creates honeycombing, seen on CT as clustered subpleural cysts at the bases.

Patients have slowly worsening exertional dyspnea and a dry cough, fine inspiratory crackles at both bases (often called velcro crackles, from stiff alveoli popping open), and digital clubbing. Complications include pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale from hypoxic vasoconstriction and loss of the capillary bed, acute exacerbations with superimposed diffuse alveolar damage, and a higher risk of lung cancer. The course is relentless, with median survival often quoted at about 3 to 5 years from diagnosis.

blocks.title: Pulmonary function in IPF and why each value changes
rows: Smaller lungs exhale a smaller volume
Recoil and radial traction hold airways open
Thick membrane and lost capillary surface
Hypoxemia and J receptors drive rapid shallow breathing
blocks.caption: The flow-volume loop is narrow and shifted toward low volumes, with flow that is high for the volume.

blocks.predict: Why is FEV1/FVC normal or even raised in IPF even though FEV1 is low?
blocks.explain: Both FEV1 and FVC fall because the lungs are small, but stiff lungs recoil strongly and scar tissue pulls airways open, so a normal or larger fraction of the reduced volume leaves in the first second.

sections.title: Pneumoconioses: coal, silica, asbestos, and beryllium

blocks.text: Particles about 1 to 5 micrometers across reach the respiratory bronchioles and alveoli, where alveolar macrophages engulf them. Disease depends on the dose retained and on what the particle does to the macrophage. Activated macrophages release cytokines (IL-1, TNF), oxidants, and fibrogenic growth factors (TGF-beta, PDGF), so the macrophage is the link between dust and fibrosis.

Coal dust is relatively inert. Anthracosis, carbon pigment in macrophages along lymphatics, is harmless and common in city dwellers. Simple coal workers pneumoconiosis forms coal macules and small nodules, mainly in the upper lobes, and causes little dysfunction. In a minority, nodules coalesce into progressive massive fibrosis, large scarred masses that impair function. Coal workers with rheumatoid arthritis may develop Caplan syndrome, large rheumatoid nodules in the lung.

Crystalline silica (sandblasting, quarrying, mining, foundries, stone cutting) is the most fibrogenic common dust. Engulfed silica damages phagolysosome membranes and activates the NLRP3 inflammasome, releasing IL-1 beta and killing the macrophage; the freed particle is taken up again and the cycle continues. Concentric, whorled hyalinized collagen nodules form in the upper lobes and hilar nodes, where calcification at the rim gives eggshell calcification on the chest film. Damaged macrophages kill mycobacteria poorly, so silicosis raises tuberculosis risk, and silica is a recognized lung carcinogen.

Asbestos (shipbuilding, insulation, roofing, brake linings, demolition) is fibrous. Long, thin amphibole fibers resist clearance and reach the lower lobes and pleura. Macrophages cannot fully engulf them and keep releasing oxidants and cytokines, so fibrosis begins around respiratory bronchioles in the lower lobes and spreads; iron and protein coat the fibers to form ferruginous bodies. Asbestos also causes calcified parietal pleural plaques (the most common lesion and a marker of exposure), bronchogenic carcinoma (the most common asbestos-related cancer, risk multiplied by smoking), and malignant mesothelioma, decades after exposure.

Beryllium (aerospace, nuclear, and electronics industries) acts differently: it is presented as an antigen, and in genetically susceptible people (certain HLA-DP alleles) it drives a Th1, type IV hypersensitivity reaction with noncaseating granulomas that resemble sarcoidosis. Because disease depends on sensitization, it can follow small exposures and is confirmed by a beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test.

blocks.title: Comparing the pneumoconioses
rows: Whorled collagen nodules; eggshell calcified hilar nodes
blocks.caption: Coal and silica favor the upper lobes; asbestos favors the lower lobes and pleura; beryllium causes a granulomatous immune disease rather than a dust-burden fibrosis.

blocks.text: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem disease of noncaseating granulomas caused by an exaggerated CD4 Th1 response to an unidentified antigen in a genetically susceptible host. Helper T cells release IL-2 and interferon gamma, which activate macrophages into epithelioid cells and giant cells, and TNF sustains the granulomas. The intrathoracic lymph nodes or lungs are involved in about 90% of patients. Granulomas may contain asteroid bodies or laminated Schaumann bodies, but these are not specific, and sarcoidosis remains a diagnosis of exclusion: infection with mycobacteria or fungi, which usually causes caseating granulomas, and berylliosis must be ruled out.

In the United States it is most common in Black women, with onset usually between 20 and 40 years, and Black patients tend to have more severe, chronic disease. The classic finding is bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest film, with or without reticulonodular interstitial disease in the upper and middle zones. Many patients have no symptoms and are found on a routine film; others have cough, dyspnea, fatigue, and fever. Lung involvement gives a restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO, though granulomas around airways can add obstruction.

Two laboratory findings come directly from granuloma macrophages. They produce angiotensin-converting enzyme, so serum ACE is often elevated, roughly in proportion to granuloma burden; it is neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose the disease. They also express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which in the kidney is tightly controlled by PTH, phosphate, and calcitriol itself, but in macrophages is driven by interferon gamma and escapes that feedback. Other findings include polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia and cutaneous anergy, because circulating T cells are sequestered in granulomas.

blocks.title: Granuloma calcitriol and hypercalcemia
steps: Interferon gamma activates granuloma macrophages
Macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol
PTH and calcium do not suppress this enzyme
Calcitriol raises intestinal calcium absorption and bone resorption
Hypercalciuria, then hypercalcemia; kidney stones and nephrocalcinosis
Parathyroid glands sense high calcium; PTH falls
blocks.caption: High calcium with a low PTH and high calcitriol points to an extrarenal source of calcitriol, as in sarcoidosis and some lymphomas.

blocks.text: Extrapulmonary disease follows the location of granulomas: anterior uveitis and other eye disease, erythema nodosum and lupus pernio (violaceous plaques on the nose and cheeks), parotid enlargement, facial nerve palsy, and cardiac sarcoidosis, which causes heart block, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden death. Lofgren syndrome is an acute presentation with erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, arthritis (often periarticular ankle inflammation), and fever. It usually resolves on its own and carries an excellent prognosis.

Restriction means total lung capacity is reduced; the FEV1/FVC ratio is normal or high because the airways are not narrowed. The defect can lie in the lung itself or in the bellows that expands it. Intrinsic (parenchymal) restriction comes from scar, inflammation, or fluid in the alveolar walls and spaces: IPF, pneumoconioses, sarcoidosis, ARDS, and drug-induced fibrosis. Extrapulmonary restriction leaves the lung normal but stops it from inflating: obesity, kyphoscoliosis, large pleural effusions or pleural thickening, and weakness of the respiratory muscles (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, high cervical cord injury, diaphragm paralysis).

DLCO and the A-a gradient separate the two groups. In intrinsic disease the membrane is thick and capillaries are lost, so DLCO falls and the A-a gradient widens. In extrapulmonary disease the membrane is normal, so DLCO is usually normal, and when DLCO is corrected for the smaller alveolar volume (KCO) it is often high. Hypoxemia in these patients comes mainly from hypoventilation: PaCO2 rises and PAO2 falls by the same mechanism, so PaO2 falls while the A-a gradient stays normal. Basal atelectasis in obesity or weakness can widen it modestly.

blocks.title: Intrinsic versus extrapulmonary restriction
rows: Normal (chest wall compliance reduced in obesity and kyphoscoliosis)
Often normal or high in muscle weakness (weak expiration)
blocks.caption: A low TLC with a low DLCO points to the lung tissue; a low TLC with a normal DLCO and high PaCO2 points to the chest bellows.

blocks.text: Obesity lowers chest wall compliance and pushes the diaphragm up, reducing expiratory reserve volume and functional residual capacity first. Obesity hypoventilation syndrome adds blunted ventilatory drive, with daytime PaCO2 above 45 mmHg in a person with a BMI of 30 or more. Weakness of the diaphragm causes a further fall in vital capacity when the patient lies supine, because the abdominal contents push the weak diaphragm upward.

blocks.title: Using the A-a gradient to locate restriction
blocks.text: Both patients breathe room air at sea level (PIO2 about 150 mmHg). Patient 1 has Guillain-Barre syndrome: PaCO2 60, PaO2 66 mmHg. PAO2 = 150 minus 60/0.8 = 75, so the A-a gradient is 75 minus 66 = 9 mmHg, normal. Hypoventilation explains the hypoxemia. Patient 2 has IPF: PaCO2 32, PaO2 60 mmHg. PAO2 = 150 minus 32/0.8 = 110, so the gradient is 110 minus 60 = 50 mmHg, widened. The lung itself is failing to transfer oxygen, which fits a thick membrane with a low DLCO.

blocks.predict: A patient with kyphoscoliosis and one with sarcoidosis both have a TLC at 65% of predicted. Which test best separates them, and what result do you expect in each?
blocks.explain: DLCO: it is usually normal in kyphoscoliosis, where the alveolar membrane is healthy, and reduced in parenchymal sarcoidosis, where granulomas and fibrosis thicken it and destroy capillaries.
blocks.check: The comparison table and the paragraph on DLCO and the A-a gradient.

sections.title: Desquamative, nonspecific, and organizing interstitial pneumonias

blocks.text: The idiopathic interstitial pneumonias are classified by histologic pattern because the pattern predicts behavior. Three patterns must be separated from UIP (section C03), and each is more reversible because its dominant lesion is cellular or young rather than dense, established scar.

Desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP) occurs almost entirely in current or former smokers, usually in their 30s to 50s. The name is a historical mistake: the cells filling the alveoli were thought to be shed epithelial cells but are macrophages containing fine golden-brown smoking pigment. The change is uniform, with only mild interstitial thickening and fibrosis. It is related to respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease, which shows the same pigmented macrophages confined to the bronchioles. Both usually improve after smoking stops.

Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) shows uniform interstitial inflammation, fibrosis, or both, all of the same age, without the patchy mix of old scar and fibroblastic foci that defines UIP. Uniformity implies a single, simultaneous injury, and NSIP is often the lung pattern of connective tissue disease (systemic sclerosis, polymyositis and dermatomyositis, rheumatoid arthritis), hypersensitivity pneumonitis, or drug toxicity. Patients are usually middle-aged, more often women, and the prognosis is better than in UIP, especially for the cellular form.

Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP), formerly bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia, shows polypoid plugs of loose, pale fibroblastic and myxoid tissue (Masson bodies) filling bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli, while the lung architecture is preserved. These plugs are organizing exudate, young tissue that can be resorbed. Patients have a subacute illness over weeks with cough, dyspnea, fever, and malaise that resembles pneumonia unresponsive to antibiotics, and the film shows patchy, often migrating consolidations. The same organizing pattern occurs secondarily after infection, drugs, radiation, or connective tissue disease; it is called cryptogenic only when no cause is found.

blocks.title: Distinguishing the interstitial pneumonia patterns
rows: Patchy subpleural and basal fibrosis of different ages; fibroblastic foci; honeycombing
Uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis of the same age
Pigmented macrophages filling alveoli; uniform, mild fibrosis
Polypoid fibroblast plugs (Masson bodies) in airspaces; architecture kept
blocks.caption: Temporal heterogeneity with fibroblastic foci means UIP; uniform change means NSIP or DIP; plugs within airspaces mean organizing pneumonia.

blocks.text: Organic dusts and toxic gases injure different levels of the respiratory tract, and the exposure history and timing point to the disease.

Byssinosis occurs in workers who process raw cotton, flax, or hemp. Contaminating bacterial endotoxin and other agents in the dust trigger airway inflammation and bronchoconstriction. The classic feature is chest tightness and dyspnea on the first day back at work after a weekend or holiday (Monday chest tightness), easing as the week goes on, a pattern attributed to tolerance with continued exposure. It is mainly an airway disease, and years of exposure can produce fixed airflow obstruction rather than fibrosis.

Bagassosis is a hypersensitivity pneumonitis (extrinsic allergic alveolitis) from moldy bagasse, the fiber left after sugarcane is crushed, contaminated with thermophilic actinomycetes. Inhaled antigen meets preformed antibody and sensitized T cells, causing type III immune complex and type IV cell-mediated injury centered on bronchioles and alveoli. Acute episodes bring fever, chills, cough, and dyspnea about 4 to 8 hours after exposure; histology shows poorly formed noncaseating granulomas and interstitial lymphocytes. It shares this mechanism with farmer's lung from moldy hay.

Silo-filler disease follows entry into a recently filled silo, where fermenting silage releases nitrogen dioxide, a heavy, poorly water-soluble gas. Because it dissolves poorly, it passes the upper airway and reaches the bronchioles and alveoli, where it forms nitric acid and oxidant radicals. Heavy exposure causes acute pulmonary edema within hours; survivors can develop bronchiolitis obliterans weeks later, with fibrous obliteration of small airways and progressive obstruction.

blocks.title: Occupational exposures beyond mineral dust
rows: Chest tightness on the first workday of the week
Fever and dyspnea hours after exposure; poorly formed granulomas
Nitrogen dioxide in a newly filled silo
Oxidant and acid injury to distal airways
Acute pulmonary edema; delayed bronchiolitis obliterans
blocks.caption: Organic antigen, endotoxin, and toxic gas each injure a different level of the airway.

blocks.text: Several drugs injure the lung parenchyma, and their effects must be separated from IPF because the cause is identifiable and the injury may stop progressing once exposure ends. The mechanisms are direct oxidant or cytotoxic injury to alveolar epithelium and endothelium, and immune-mediated hypersensitivity. Histology is varied and often not UIP: NSIP, organizing pneumonia, diffuse alveolar damage, or hypersensitivity patterns, which itself suggests a drug rather than IPF.

blocks.title: Drugs that cause interstitial lung disease
rows: Generates oxygen free radicals that break DNA; lung and skin have little bleomycin hydrolase to inactivate it
Dose related; worse with older age, renal impairment, high inspired oxygen, and chest radiation
Iodinated, lipophilic drug accumulates in lung; direct toxicity and phospholipidosis
Foamy macrophages; related to cumulative dose; high-density opacities on CT from iodine
Alkylating cytotoxic injury to type II pneumocytes
Atypical type II pneumocytes; can appear months to years later
Subacute cough, fever, dyspnea; poorly formed granulomas; sometimes eosinophilia; not clearly dose related
Acute febrile reaction with eosinophilia, or slow fibrosis with long-term use
blocks.caption: A cytotoxic drug or antiarrhythmic in the history and a non-UIP pattern point away from IPF.

blocks.text: Bleomycin is the best example of mechanism. It forms a complex with iron and oxygen that produces free radicals and cleaves DNA. Most tissues contain bleomycin hydrolase, which inactivates the drug, but lung and skin contain little, so these are the sites of toxicity. Damaged endothelium and type I pneumocytes trigger the same TGF-beta driven fibrosis seen in IPF. High inspired oxygen is thought to supply more substrate for radical formation, which would explain why oxygen exposure worsens the injury.

Clues that point to a drug rather than IPF include the timeline (onset after a drug is started or a cumulative dose is reached), younger age, fever or peripheral eosinophilia, the histologic pattern, and stabilization when the drug is stopped. Radiation pneumonitis, which follows chest irradiation within weeks to months, causes a similar oxidant injury confined to the radiation field.

integration.text: Each restrictive disease begins at a different structural level, and the level predicts the physiology. Surfactant failure in NRDS and barrier failure in ARDS fill or collapse perfused alveoli, so shunt dominates and oxygen helps little. Fibrosis in IPF, asbestosis, silicosis, and drug injury thickens the membrane, so DLCO falls and hypoxemia worsens with exercise as transit time shortens. Chest wall and muscle disease leave the membrane intact, so the problem is hypoventilation with a normal A-a gradient. Immunology adds the granulomatous diseases: sarcoidosis, berylliosis, and hypersensitivity pneumonitis share Th1-driven macrophage activation, and the same activated macrophages explain the ACE and calcitriol findings in sarcoidosis.

Pathology and biochemistry unite the fibrosing diseases through one final pathway, TGF-beta driven fibroblast activation after epithelial injury, whether the trigger is unknown (IPF), mineral (silica, asbestos), oxidant (bleomycin, oxygen, nitrogen dioxide), or diffuse alveolar damage that fails to resolve. The pattern of the scar (patchy and of mixed age, uniform, or confined to airspaces) is the clue to cause and course. These distinctions have limits: patterns overlap, a single biopsy may miss patchy disease, and exposure history often decides between conditions that look alike under the microscope.

summary: Restriction lowers TLC with a normal or high FEV1/FVC; a low DLCO places the problem in the lung tissue, a normal DLCO with high PaCO2 places it in the chest wall or muscles.

NRDS is surfactant deficiency (prematurity, maternal diabetes, cesarean without labor) causing atelectasis, shunt, and hyaline membranes; hypoxemia keeps the ductus open, and oxygen therapy contributes to bronchopulmonary dysplasia and retinopathy of prematurity.

ARDS is neutrophil-mediated injury to the alveolar-capillary barrier after sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, trauma, or pancreatitis, with protein-rich edema, hyaline membranes, bilateral opacities, PaO2/FiO2 of 300 or less, and normal left heart pressures.

IPF is failed epithelial repair with TGF-beta driven fibrosis; UIP is patchy subpleural and basal scar of different ages with fibroblastic foci and honeycombing, causing clubbing, basal crackles, and low DLCO.

Coal and silica favor the upper lobes; silica kills macrophages, calcifies hilar nodes like eggshells, and raises tuberculosis risk; asbestos favors the lower lobes and pleura with ferruginous bodies, plaques, carcinoma, and mesothelioma.

Berylliosis and sarcoidosis both form noncaseating granulomas from Th1 responses; sarcoidosis gives bilateral hilar nodes, high ACE, and hypercalcemia from unregulated macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase with suppressed PTH.
Lofgren syndrome (erythema nodosum, hilar lymphadenopathy, arthritis, fever) is acute sarcoidosis with a good prognosis.
DIP is smokers with pigmented macrophages in alveoli; NSIP is uniform inflammation and fibrosis linked to connective tissue disease; COP is reversible fibroblast plugs (Masson bodies) in airspaces.

Byssinosis is cotton dust bronchoconstriction worst on the first workday; bagassosis is hypersensitivity pneumonitis from moldy sugarcane; silo-filler disease is nitrogen dioxide edema followed by bronchiolitis obliterans.
Bleomycin, amiodarone, busulfan, methotrexate, and nitrofurantoin cause drug-induced lung disease that is separated from IPF by history, timing, and a usually non-UIP pattern.

verify: The gestational age at which surfactant production begins is quoted from about 20 to 24 weeks and maturity from about 34 to 36 weeks; confirm the values NABNE expects.
The ARDS criteria follow the 2012 Berlin definition; a 2023 global definition broadens criteria (for example SpO2/FiO2 and high-flow oxygen); confirm which definition NABNE uses.
The upper-lobe predominance of coal and silica and lower-lobe predominance of asbestos are consensus teaching; lobe predilection for berylliosis varies among sources and is not stated here.
Serum ACE elevation in sarcoidosis is quoted in roughly 40% to 80% of patients and hypercalcemia in roughly 10% to 20%; exact percentages vary by source and are not stated as fact here.
Byssinosis is attributed to endotoxin and other cotton dust agents; the exact causal agent remains debated.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the older term BOOP alongside cryptogenic organizing pneumonia, and the eponyms Caplan syndrome, Masson bodies, Schaumann bodies, and asteroid bodies.
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome criteria (BMI of 30 or more and awake PaCO2 above 45 mmHg) follow common consensus; confirm if tested.
